name: Philippines
headline: Filipino patients have strong privacy rights on paper, but records stay hospital by hospital and a shared exchange is still a pilot.

access.summary: The Data Privacy Act gives a right of access and a structured electronic copy, but no fixed deadline is in force and one city hospital's rules release only parts of the record. Base 45, +5 structured copy, -5 no fixed deadline, -5 limited scope = 40.
detail: Section 16(c) of the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173) gives reasonable access, on demand, to the contents of processed personal data, its sources and its recipients. Section 18 gives a right to a copy in an electronic, structured and commonly used format.

A National Privacy Commission draft circular on data subject rights (September 2026) would set a 30-day deadline and limit copy fees to actual costs. It lists discharge summaries, lab results, diagnoses and prescriptions as covered. It is still a draft, so no deadline binds today.

Practice is narrower than the law. A city-run hospital in Cagayan de Oro lets patients view the record only with staff present, excludes psychiatric notes, and releases only certain parts on written request. A DOH medical center promises a copy except records restricted by law.
No national portal shows a patient's medical record. The UHC Act requires electronic health records, but a patient-facing view was not verified.

control.summary: By law a patient can ask any provider who received their data and when it was last accessed (RA 10173 Section 16(c)), but only on request; practice was not verified. UHC Act Section 31 makes every provider send health data to PhilHealth, with no consent step.
detail: Health records are sensitive personal information. Section 13 bans processing except with specific consent or listed exceptions, including medical treatment by a practitioner, processing provided for by law, and legal claims.

Section 16(c) lets the patient demand the names of recipients, the reasons for disclosure, and the date the data was last accessed and modified. That is an access record on request, not a log the patient can open. How often hospitals honour such requests was not verified.

DOH Administrative Order 2020-0030 requires a consent form at admission, and limits record access to the attending provider. It also orders providers to give the DOH unimpeded access during outbreaks and emergencies.

Section 31 of the Universal Health Care Act (RA 11223) requires all public and private health entities to submit administrative, public health, medical, pharmaceutical and financing data to PhilHealth, which copies it to the DOH. The law gives no consent step and no opt-out.

privacy.summary: The law is strict, with an independent regulator, 72-hour breach notice and up to 6 years in prison for misusing health data. But the 2023 PhilHealth breach exposed records of 42 million people, and in September 2026 a GenSan hospital reportedly admitted a ransomware breach (not verified).
detail: RA 10173 creates the National Privacy Commission (NPC) as an independent body attached to the ICT department. Unauthorized processing of sensitive data carries 3 to 6 years in prison and PHP 500,000 to 4 million in fines (Section 25).
The NPC requires controllers to notify both the Commission and affected people within 72 hours of learning of a breach, through its online notification system.

In July 2024 the NPC told Congress that the September 2023 PhilHealth breach affected 42 million people, including patient medical records. Asked whether those people had been told of the breach, PhilHealth's chief operating officer answered no.

MindaNews reported that on 25 September 2026 General Santos Doctors Hospital admitted a data breach after the Rhysida group claimed 2.44 terabytes, including medical, pathology and dialysis records (not verified: the page did not open on 2 October 2026).

commercial.summary: Health data cannot be processed on legitimate interest, so marketing with it needs specific consent, and disclosing it without consent carries 3 to 5 years in prison. There is no rule on de-identified data sales or data brokers.
detail: Section 13 of RA 10173 lists the only lawful grounds for processing sensitive data such as health records. Commercial marketing is not one of them, so it needs specific prior consent.
NPC Circular 2023-04 bars bundling consent for extra processing with a service, and makes consent withdrawal absolute when marketing rests on consent.

Disclosing sensitive data to a third party without consent carries 3 to 5 years in prison and up to PHP 2 million (Section 32). Penalties reach their maximum when 100 or more people are affected (Section 35).
No specific rule on selling de-identified health data, on data brokers, or on consumer health apps outside the clinic was found.

journey.summary: Claims and primary care data flow to PhilHealth: eClaims 3.0 became mandatory on 1 July 2026 and YAKAP clinics must use certified EMRs. A provider-to-provider exchange exists only as a pilot, with a first eReferral prototype due in January 2027.
detail: Section 36 of the UHC Act requires every provider and insurer to keep electronic health records and an electronic prescription log. Section 31 sends administrative, medical, pharmaceutical and financing data to PhilHealth. PhilHealth names its National Health Data Repository as the integration target for YAKAP clinic records.

PhilHealth made eClaims 3.0 mandatory for all accredited facilities from 1 July 2026. YAKAP primary care clinics must move to a PhilHealth-certified EMR, with the old eKonsulta system kept open until 31 December 2026.

There is no working provider-to-provider exchange. In a June 2026 test in Aklan, 11 of 13 EMR teams exchanged synthetic referrals using draft national standards. The province plans an eReferral prototype in January 2027.
A March 2026 presidential order created a group to run PhilHealth's digital transformation under the 2025 E-Governance Act.

clinical.summary: A treating doctor can use records without separate consent, but only those held in their own facility. No cross-provider clinical view was verified, and the first eReferral prototype starts in one Aklan town in January 2027.
detail: Section 13(e) of RA 10173 allows processing for medical treatment by a practitioner or institution, so the law does not block clinician access.
DOH Administrative Order 2020-0030 limits access to the provider directly attending the patient, with a signed consent form. Records stay with the facility that created them.

In a June 2026 test, receiving facilities could open a full referral package before the patient arrived, using synthetic data. The standards used are drafts not yet meant for production. The Aklan exchange plans an eReferral prototype in Ibajay in January 2027, then a phased provincial rollout.

research.summary: Research data falls largely outside the Data Privacy Act with no opt-out, though it must be held under strict confidentiality and a statutory ethics board oversees 114 accredited ethics committees. Base 40, +3 ethics body, +3 statutory confidentiality = 46.
detail: Section 4(d) of RA 10173 excludes personal information processed for research from the Act. Section 19 suspends data subject rights for scientific and statistical research, provided the data is kept under strict confidentiality and used only for the declared purpose.
UHC Act Section 31 sends health data submitted to PhilHealth on to the DOH for research and policy. There is no individual consent or opt-out for this.

The Philippine National Health Research System Act (RA 10532, 2013) gives the Philippine Health Research Ethics Board power to set ethics guidelines and monitor ethics committees. Its register lists 114 accredited committees.
DOH AO 2020-0030 requires research on health information to follow the national ethics guidelines. No public register of data uses was found.

ai.summary: Medical software falls under the FDA's 2018 device rules, but the rules written for AI software are still a draft, revised for consultation in August 2026. The privacy regulator's 2024 AI advisory requires human intervention in automated decisions.
detail: The FDA's draft circular on medical device software builds on Administrative Order 2018-0002, the ASEAN-harmonized device rules. It defines an AI medical device and sets risk classes. Comments on the first draft closed on 20 July 2025.

A consultancy reports that a revised draft went to public consultation on 27 August 2026. It adds risk factors such as autonomy, whether the algorithm keeps learning after release, and explainability. It excludes clinical decision support that a clinician can check independently.
NPC Advisory 2024-04 applies the Data Privacy Act to AI systems that process personal data. It requires transparency and meaningful human intervention where automated decisions pose significant risk.
No binding change-control rule for AI medical devices was found.
